Sources beside the text.

The manuscripts, historical references and earlier work that guided our research.

  1. Marie de’ Medici to Brèves, 15 September 1610

    BnF, Manuscripts department, Français 3789, f. 17r. Local image supplied by Brice, Gallica frame 32.

    View on Gallica ↗

  2. Marie de’ Medici to Brèves, 10 November 1610

    BnF, Manuscripts department, Français 3789, f. 19r. Local image supplied by Brice, Gallica frame 36.

    View on Gallica ↗

  3. Key used for the comparisons

    BnF, Français 3462, frame 112. Satoshi confirms this key image for Henri IV–Brèves. Its exact application to Marie’s letters remains to be checked.

    View the key on Gallica ↗

  4. The 1610 succession and regency

    Château de Versailles, “Louis XIII”. Background on Henri IV’s death, Louis XIII’s accession and Marie de’ Medici’s regency. Consulted 16 October 2026; used for context, not to establish the cipher.

    Read the entry ↗

  5. Savoy and the Bruzolo agreements

    Les États de Savoie (1416–1861), Classiques Garnier, 2019, p. 233 onwards. University of Turin IRIS excerpt.

    Read the excerpt ↗

  6. Catalogue description of Français 3789

    BnF description reproduced by Biblissima: Marie’s letters of 15 September and 10 November 1610 are items 11 and 12. Used to check identification and the collection’s setting.

    Read the catalogue ↗

  7. Satoshi Tomokiyo — Cryptiana

    Satoshi Tomokiyo’s pages on the ciphers of Henri IV and Louis XIII helped identify Marie de’ Medici’s two letters and directed the search towards Brèves’s ciphers and Français 3462. Earlier work on Henri IV’s letter of 5 January 1610 is distinct from this decipherment of Marie’s letters.

    Cryptiana — Regent Marie de Medici ↗
    Cryptiana — Ciphers of Henry IV ↗

    Feedback from Satoshi Tomokiyo supplied on 17 October 2026. He confirms the Français 3462 image and the mistyped “3642” shelfmark, and supplies matching values for QUE, RE, SE and TION. This contribution supports six numerical occurrences; it does not validate the whole reading of Marie’s passages.

  8. Daniel Bourdeau — catalogue and comparative transcription

    Entry 25 in Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue helped locate the dossier. His transcription of both passages also served as a comparison for our initial reading of the signs. We cite those documentary contributions; his earlier attempt had not yielded the passages’ plaintext.

    Read the catalogue ↗

  9. George Lasry and Satoshi Tomokiyo — “Savary de Brèves” report and list of unsolved ciphers

    George Lasry’s report on the cipher of Henry IV and Marie de’ Medici to Savary de Brèves (1610), received and published by Satoshi Tomokiyo on Cryptiana on 21 October 2026: independent reading of the 10 November passage (sign 4 = Sa Sainteté, an N sign added to the key). Cryptiana’s “Unsolved” list marks Marie de’ Medici’s cipher (1610) as solved.

    Read the report ↗ · Cryptiana list ↗

  10. Daniel Bourdeau — catalogue and write-up “Marie de’ Medici → Savary de Brèves, 1610”

    Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue now lists entry 25 (BnF Français 3789, ff. 17r and 19r; DECODE R2075/R2076) as read with a key from external sources (20 October 2026); his write-up and contributors page credit the decipherment of both passages, with the Français 3462 key, to our reading.

    Read the write-up ↗ · Catalogue ↗

    Österreichisches Staatsarchiv, Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv, StAbt Türkei I 2-2-19, fols. 60–61 (AT-OeStA/HHStA StAbt Türkei I 2-2-19). The online inventory describes it as a partly enciphered letter from “N.N.”, the sender’s name being in cipher. Images viewable on the AIS; not reproduced here, as they carry no open licence.

    HHStA, StAbt Türkei I 2-2-9 (fols. 20–21a) and 2-2-24 (fols. 118–119): contemporary glosses above the cipher groups, the only source of the table applied to 2-2-19. Independent check against the table from the glosses of 1542 (Bourdeau catalogue no. 499).

    Edition of Austro-Ottoman documents from 1526 to 1541, searched in full text (Internet Archive): Ferducci’s letter is not printed; the 1531–1532 volume notes that Antonio Rincon brought to Venice, on 20 August 1532, a copy of Süleyman’s letter to Ferdinand of 12 July.

    See the volume (Internet Archive) ↗

  15. Charles XII to the Rådet and to the envoys Leijoncrona and Palmquist, Bender, 26 April 1710

    Niedersächsisches Landesarchiv, Abt. Stade, Rep. 5a Nr. 670 (old shelfmark Fach 76 Nr. 38), fols. 83–85: two ciphered copies, with no key or decipherment, in the file “Diverse chiffrierte Schreiben von und an Generalgouverneur Baron Nils Gyllenstierna” (1700–1711). NLA digitisation released under the Public Domain Mark 1.0; two crops are reproduced in the record. The key was rebuilt from a troop list in the same file (fols. 73, 74, 82).

Earlier work and this first decipherment

The research dossier follows leads recorded by S. Tomokiyo, Klaus Schmeh and Daniel Bourdeau. It also mentions earlier work by George Lasry, Norbert Biermann and S. Tomokiyo on a letter from Henri IV to Brèves, relevant to identifying the key. This site does not claim their work as its own.

To our knowledge, this site presents a first decipherment of Marie de’ Medici’s two passages. Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue, checked on 16 October 2026, then listed the 10 November letter as “attempted, open”, with its 15 September sibling; since 20 October it lists both as read and credits our decipherment.[10] Cryptiana also lists them as undeciphered in the consulted references. This statement concerns Marie’s letters, distinct from Henri IV’s letter studied by Lasry, Biermann and Tomokiyo. Some characters remain probable but unconfirmed.

Daniel Bourdeau · Catalogue · Cryptiana · Regent Marie de Medici

Ferducci, 1532. For the Fiume letter of 19 July 1532, checked on 27 October 2026: no published reading in Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue (no. 498), on Cryptiana, in Gévay or in a web search. This is a new reading of an unglossed piece; most other pieces in the same file carry a contemporary decipherment.[13]

Charles XII, 1710. For the Bender letter of 26 April 1710, checked on 27 October 2026: no reading or edition found in Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue (no. 599), in Konung Karl XII:s egenhändiga bref (1893), in the Handlingar rörande Skandinaviens historia or by web search. We publish a reading of the Stade cipher copies; the clear copy received by the Council is probably kept in the Riksarkivet, Stockholm, and has not been consulted.[16]

Høeg, 1675. For the eleven dispatches to Just Høeg from 2 January to 9 February 1675, checked on 27 October 2026 (and again the same day for the eight letters of 12 January to 9 February): no published reading in Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue (no. 465), on Cryptiana, in a web search (Høeg, Meyercrone, Biermann 1675), Danske Magazin, Fridericia or Aktstykker. Clear drafts probably survive in the German Chancery series and the received copies in Høeg’s papers; we know of no edition. Rigsarkivet images are not reproduced.[no. 465]

Duplessis-Mornay, 1593. For the figures in the letters of Du Maurier and Serviez, checked 27 October 2026: the 1824 editors had no key; no published reading in Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue (no. 371, “open”) or repository, on Cryptiana or by web search. The two-letters-per-group hypothesis is Daniel Bourdeau’s.[no. 371]

Vila Flor, 1663. For Afonso VI’s ciphered letter to the Count of Vila Flor of 26 May 1663, checked on 27 October 2026: no published reading in Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue (no. 391) or by web search; Ericeira (1698, 1751 ed.) does not quote the letter, which he alludes to among the King’s “repeated orders”; the blog Guerra da Restauração publishes Vila Flor’s letter to the King of the same day, not this one. For the letters of 13 and 15 May 1663, re-checked the same day: Ericeira, book VIII, pp. 514–521, neither prints nor paraphrases these orders; the blog Guerra da Restauração (posts on 14–31 May 1663) does not quote them; nothing on the web. For the long letter of 15 May 1663, checked the same day: Ericeira, book VIII, pp. 514–528, neither prints nor paraphrases it (no place of arms at Setúbal, no 44,000 cruzados, no sending to Montemor); the blog and the web do not quote it; no. 391 is still “open”. Álvares da Cunha’s account (1663) has not been checked in full text. ANTT images are not reproduced.[no. 391]

Puebla, 1506. For Doctor de Puebla’s letter to Almazán of 21 April 1506, checked on 27 October 2026: Cryptiana lists it among the “First Cipher” letters, without a reading; the Calendar of State Papers, Spain I (1862) and its Supplement (1868) neither print nor summarise it; Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue (no. 617) lists it as “open”; nothing on the web. The reading of the cipher passages is new; the key is Satoshi Tomokiyo’s.[617b]

Everett, 1825. For the six cipher lines of the notes of 25 September 1825, checked on 27 October 2026: Manning (1925) prints them “without decodification”; the extract sent to Congress in 1826 (Register of Debates, Executive Proceedings of the Senate, American State Papers, Foreign Relations V, no. 418) gives in clear only their first clause (“I did not think it necessary to enter very fully into the argument with Mr. Zea.”); the Papers of Henry Clay, vol. 4 (1972), summarise the despatch; full-text search (Internet Archive, Google Books) and web search find the rest nowhere; entry no. 638 is “open”. The unpublished part (53 of 74 groups) is therefore published here for the first time, to our knowledge.[no. 638]

Credits and reuse

The editorial model and visual principles follow Wenmi, by Brice Dudout with Claude: paper background, reading typography, history, method and inspectable documents. This implementation has its own files and does not modify Wenmi.

Images from the Austrian State Archives (AIS) are not reproduced: the site links to the online inventory. Original edition text and code: CC BY 4.0. Facsimiles are from BnF / Gallica and retain their separate reuse conditions; the site licence does not replace them. No archive image was generated by AI. The two Simancas images (AGS, PTR,LEG,54,78) are reproduced under the PARES conditions: Ministerio de Cultura (España), Archivo General de Simancas.

Two atmosphere illustrations were generated with imagegen: a writing desk and a courier towards Rome. Their captions identify them; they are not historical evidence. The manuscript-letter logo is a vector drawing made for this site.
